title: Oz Lotto Statistics (Australia)
description:
Oz Lotto is Australia's national Tuesday-night jackpot game, first drawn in 1994 as the country's first fully national lotto game. It is run by The Lottery Corporation under The Lott brand in most jurisdictions and by Lotterywest in Western Australia. The minimum Division 1 prize pool is $2 million.

Since May 17, 2022, the game uses a 7-from-47 matrix: seven winning numbers plus three supplementary numbers are drawn from the same barrel. The Division 1 odds for one game are 1 in 62,891,499, which is exactly the number of ways to choose 7 numbers from 47. Seven prize divisions pay down to matching three winning numbers plus a supplementary number, and supplementary numbers matter only in Divisions 2, 4, and 7.

Oz Lotto is the caution case for matrix dates in this pair: older tables showing 7 from 45, with Division 1 odds of 1 in 45,379,620, describe the former matrix, not the current game. Any archive row dated before May 2022 must be read against the matrix then in force. Lottery outcomes are random. Every combination has the same chance in a fair draw, past draws do not change the next draw, and no selection method changes the odds. No predictive winning method exists.
matrix: 7 numbers from 1 to 47, plus 3 supplementary numbers
source: Current 7/47 matrix since 17 May 2022 and prize table published by lottopark.com; launch history from oz-lotteries.com
data_note: Demo computes odds from the published matrix; no real draw history is presented.

demo.code:
import math

TITLE = "Oz Lotto"


def main():
    print(TITLE + " - odds check")
    print("Current combinations C(47,7): " + format(math.comb(47, 7), ","))
    print("Former combinations C(45,7): " + format(math.comb(45, 7), ","))
    print("Combinations added by the change: " + format(math.comb(47, 7) - math.comb(45, 7), ","))
    print("Randomness: every combination has the same chance in a fair draw.")


main()
demo.expected_output:
Oz Lotto - odds check
Current combinations C(47,7): 62,891,499
Former combinations C(45,7): 45,379,620
Combinations added by the change: 17,511,879
Randomness: every combination has the same chance in a fair draw.

title: Powerball Australia Statistics
description:
Powerball Australia is Australia's national Thursday-night jackpot game. It is a different game from Powerball in the United States, with a different matrix and different prizes. The current format, in place since April 2018, uses seven main numbers from 1 to 35 and one Powerball from a separate pool of 1 to 20. The minimum Division 1 jackpot is reported at A$4 million.

The Division 1 odds for one standard game are 1 in 134,490,400, which is the number of ways to choose 7 numbers from 35 multiplied by the 20 Powerball choices. Nine divisions pay down to matching two main numbers plus the Powerball, and the overall odds of any prize are about 1 in 44.

Australian Powerball is the longest-odds game in this pair, which is why its jackpots grow the largest. Longer odds are not a flaw in the game; they are the arithmetic consequence of a larger combination count. Lottery outcomes are random. Every combination has the same chance in a fair draw, past draws do not change the next draw, and no selection method changes the odds. No predictive winning method exists.

title: Saturday Lotto Statistics (Australia)
description:
Saturday Lotto is Australia's nationwide Saturday-night game, known as TattsLotto in Victoria, Tasmania, and the Northern Territory, Gold Lotto in Queensland, and X Lotto in South Australia. It was first introduced in Victoria in 1972 and expanded to all Australian states by 2013. The Division 1 prize pool is typically advertised around $5 million, with larger Superdraw and Megadraw pools during special events.

Each Saturday, eight balls are drawn from a barrel of 45: the first six are the winning numbers and the last two are supplementary numbers. The Division 1 odds for one game are 1 in 8,145,060, which is exactly the number of ways to choose 6 numbers from 45. Six divisions pay down to matching three winning numbers, and supplementary numbers decide Divisions 2 and 5.

Saturday Lotto is the shortest-odds jackpot game in this pair, which makes it a useful baseline: any international comparison that ranks games only by jackpot size, without noting that this game's odds are roughly sixteen times shorter than Australian Powerball's, is incomplete. Lottery outcomes are random. Every combination has the same chance in a fair draw, past draws do not change the next draw, and no selection method changes the odds. title: German Lotto 6aus49 Statistics

title: International Comparison: Matrices and Odds Method
description:
International comparison starts with the same method as the state comparison: record the matrix, the matrix date, and the combination count per line, and convert to a common basis before ranking. Across this pair, jackpot odds run from about 1 in 3.8 million for New Zealand Lotto to about 1 in 134.5 million for Powerball Australia. That range is driven entirely by pool sizes and second pools, not by country or by jackpot size.

Three adjustments are needed before any cross-country ranking. First, separate single-pool games, two-pool games, same-pool bonus games, and fixed-odds wheel games, because their odds are computed differently. Second, state whether the figure is per line, per play, or per dollar, since minimum lines and prices differ. Third, keep currency out of the odds ranking: a jackpot in euros, reais, or yen cannot be ranked against a jackpot in dollars without a conversion, and conversions move daily.

The method's output is a table with one row per game: matrix, matrix date, jackpot odds, overall odds, and prize structure type. Any comparison missing the matrix date is incomplete, because at least three games in this pair changed matrix in recent years. Lottery outcomes are random. Every combination has the same chance in a fair draw, past draws do not change the next draw, and no selection method changes the odds. No predictive winning method exists.

title: Jackpot Caps Across Countries: General Information
description:
Jackpot caps take three forms. A money cap sets a maximum jackpot amount, as in German Lotto 6aus49, where the jackpot is capped at 50 million euros. A rollover cap sets a maximum number of rollovers, as in French Loto, where the jackpot rolls down to the next tier after 34 consecutive rollovers without a jackpot winner. A must-be-won rule sets a cap with a forced payout, as in New Zealand Powerball, where the jackpot becomes a Must Be Won draw at NZ$60 million.

Uncapped games take the opposite approach. California SuperLotto Plus has no rollover cap, so its jackpot keeps growing until won, and New York Lotto likewise has no cap. Uncapped games can therefore reach very large jackpots after long rollover runs, while capped games pay out sooner and more often at the cap boundary.

Caps matter for statistics work because they change the tail of the jackpot distribution: a capped game's jackpot sizes cluster at or below the cap, while an uncapped game's sizes have a long upper tail. Any average jackpot figure that mixes capped and uncapped games without noting the cap is misleading. Lottery outcomes are random. Every combination has the same chance in a fair draw, past draws do not change the next draw, and no selection method changes the odds. No predictive winning method exists.

title: Currency and Payout Variation: General Information Only
description:
International prizes are paid in the currency of the country where the ticket was sold: euros in Germany, France, and Spain; reais in Brazil; yen in Japan; rand in South Africa; Australian dollars in Australia; New Zealand dollars in New Zealand. Headline jackpots in different currencies cannot be ranked without conversion, and a conversion done on one date will differ from a conversion done on another date. This record therefore ranks games by odds, not by converted jackpot size.

Payout form also varies by country. Some games pay lump sums only, some offer an annuity or a lump-sum choice, and some pay lifetime prizes with a cash option, as in the multi-state life-prize games. Tax treatment varies too: lottery prizes are tax-free in Germany and in New Zealand under local law, while in the United States federal withholding of 24 percent applies to prizes over $5,000 and state tax varies by state. This record is general information only, not tax advice.

Lottery outcomes are random. Every combination has the same chance in a fair draw, past draws do not change the next draw, and no selection method changes the odds. title: Verification Guide: Official Sources by Country
description:
The verification rule is the same in every country: the operator's own results archive is the primary source, and every other listing is a copy to be checked against it. For the United States, the primary source is the state lottery that runs the game, such as the New York Lottery, the California Lottery, the Florida Lottery, the Texas Lottery, the Pennsylvania Lottery, the New Jersey Lottery, the Ohio Lottery, the Michigan Lottery, the Illinois Lottery, or the Georgia Lottery. For multi-state games, the participating state lotteries publish the same draw, so a draw can be cross-checked across states.

For the international games in this pair, the primary sources are: The Lott and Lotterywest for Australian games; the state lottery companies for German Lotto 6aus49; La Francaise des Jeux (FDJ) for French Loto; Caixa Economica Federal for Mega-Sena; the Japan lottery operator for Loto 6; Ithuba for South Africa Lotto; SELAE for La Primitiva; the Italy Lotto operator for the wheel draws; and Lotto New Zealand for New Zealand Lotto. Each operator publishes results, rules, and prize breakdowns for its own games.

A verification pass records four things for every claim: the game, the draw date, the operator source checked, and the date checked. Claims without those four items should be treated as unverified, however widely they are repeated. Lottery outcomes are random. Every combination has the same chance in a fair draw, past draws do not change the next draw, and no selection method changes the odds. No predictive winning method exists.

title: Responsible Play and Common Fallacies
description:
The fallacies in international play are the same as in state play, with one addition: the currency fallacy, which treats a large-looking foreign jackpot as a large prize without converting currency, tax, and payout form. The other four are the gambler's fallacy (a number is due), the hot-number fallacy (a frequent number is more likely), the pattern fallacy (birthdays or shapes are special), and the system fallacy (a selection method beats the odds). None of them changes the combination count of any game in this pair.

A second international trap is the matrix-date trap: quoting an old matrix for a game that has changed, such as Oz Lotto before May 2022, New Jersey Pick-6 before April 2022, or New Zealand Powerball before September 2026. An odds figure without a matrix date is not a verified odds figure.

Responsible play note: treat lottery play as entertainment with a fixed spending limit, never as income or a way to recover losses. Help is available from local problem-gambling support services for anyone who feels play is no longer under control. Lottery outcomes are random. Every combination has the same chance in a fair draw, past draws do not change the next draw, and no selection method changes the odds. No predictive winning method exists.

import random

TITLE = "Fallacy check"
random.seed(20261026)


def main():
    print(TITLE + " - labeled simulated draws")
    draws = [set(random.sample(range(1, 46), 6)) for _ in range(5000)]
    after_absence = 0
    hits_after_absence = 0
    for i in range(1, len(draws)):
        if 7 not in draws[i - 1]:
            after_absence += 1
            if 7 in draws[i]:
                hits_after_absence += 1
    print('Draws following a draw without 7: ' + str(after_absence))
    print('Of those, draws containing 7: ' + str(hits_after_absence))
    print('Rate x1000: ' + str(hits_after_absence * 1000 // after_absence))
    print('Fair-draw rate x1000 (6 / 45): ' + str(6 * 1000 // 45))
    print('Reading: absence did not make 7 more likely; the rate stays near the fair-draw rate.')
    print("SIMULATED DATA: these draws are generated for teaching only, not real draw history.")


main()
